questions.prompt: Match each folder in a conventional project to what belongs in it.
right: The code the project is for
The code that checks the code
questions.explain: The layout is a convention, not a rule Python enforces. Its value is that a stranger can guess where anything lives.

questions.prompt: Which module filename follows Python's naming convention?
questions.explain: Modules and functions use lowercase with underscores. The hyphen is not merely unconventional: a name with a hyphen in it cannot be imported.

questions.prompt: Which of these make a project easier for someone else to pick up?
choices: Each module doing one clearly named job
Tests kept beside the code they test
A README saying how to run it
Every function in a single long file so nothing is missed
questions.explain: One long file is the thing the structure exists to avoid. Nothing is missed there because nothing can be found.

questions.prompt: Why keep configuration values in one module rather than scattered through the code?
choices: There is one place to change them, and one place to look
It makes the values load faster
questions.explain: Same reason as a function: a value written once is a value that can be changed once. Scattered copies drift apart quietly.
